questions.stem: In the study of a large city, the 'spatial dimensions' of the city refer to:
options: the number of people who were born in the city rather than migrating there
the height of its tallest buildings compared with those of other cities
the total value of goods and services the city produces in one year
its location, extent, shape and the pattern of land uses across it
questions.explanation: Spatial dimensions describe where the city is, how far it extends and how its land uses, such as the CBD, industry and housing, are arranged. Birthplace and output are demographic and economic characteristics.

questions.stem: A large city has several major business centres spread across the metropolitan area rather than one dominant CBD. Its urban structure is best described as:
options: polycentric
monocentric
linear
dispersed rural
questions.explanation: A polycentric city has multiple centres of employment and services. A monocentric city has one dominant CBD, which often causes long commutes as the city grows.

questions.stem: In many large cities in developing countries, informal settlements are found on steep slopes, floodplains and beside railway lines. The main reason is that:
options: informal settlement residents prefer hazardous sites because rents are higher
these sites have the best water and sewerage connections in the whole city
such land is often unclaimed or hazardous, so poor migrants can occupy it
planners zone the safest, most central land specifically for informal housing
questions.explanation: Low-income migrants who cannot afford formal housing occupy marginal land that is unused because it is risky or unwanted, which increases their exposure to floods and landslides.

questions.stem: The informal sector of a city's economy is best described as:
options: work done only by volunteers for charities and community organisations
unregistered, untaxed work such as street vending and recycling
work in government offices, banks and large transnational corporations
work in heavy industry under long-term contracts with trade unions
questions.explanation: Informal work is not registered or regulated, offers little security and is often the main source of income for recent migrants. Banks, government and unionised industry are part of the formal sector.

questions.stem: Mumbai is located on India's west coast, on the Arabian Sea. Its original site was:
options: a high plateau at the foot of the Himalaya mountain range
the delta of the Ganges River, at the head of the Bay of Bengal
a group of seven islands, later joined by land reclamation
a broad inland plain, far from the coast and any harbour
questions.explanation: Mumbai's seven islands were joined into one landmass by reclamation from the 18th and 19th centuries. Its natural harbour helped it grow into a major port under British rule.

questions.stem: Mumbai's main peninsula is long and narrow, with the sea on three sides and the historic CBD at its southern tip. What is the main effect of this shape on the city?
options: short commutes, because every suburb lies close to the southern CBD
unlimited room for the CBD to expand outwards in every direction
very low land values in the south, where land is most plentiful
long north-south commutes on a few crowded transport corridors
questions.explanation: With growth pushed northwards, most people live far from the southern CBD, so commuter rail and roads running north-south are severely overcrowded, and land in the south is scarce and very expensive.

questions.stem: From the 1970s, a planned 'twin city' was developed on the mainland across the harbour from Mumbai. The main purpose of Navi Mumbai was to:
options: replace Mumbai as India's national capital and seat of the central government
create a reserve for rural agriculture where no urban development is allowed
house only foreign visitors and international workers employed in Mumbai
relieve congestion on the peninsula by providing new land for homes and jobs
questions.explanation: Navi Mumbai was planned to take population and economic activity off the crowded island city. Its growth has been helped by new links such as the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, opened in 2024.

questions.stem: Greater Mumbai, the municipal area, had a population of about 12 million at India's 2011 census, while the wider metropolitan region holds many more. Why do population figures for large cities vary so much between sources?
options: large cities are never included in national censuses, so all figures are guesses
population figures for cities are only collected once every hundred years
most large cities lose half their population each year, so figures change daily
sources use different boundaries, from the municipality to the region
questions.explanation: The population depends on whether the boundary is the city proper, the urban agglomeration or the metropolitan region. Always check which definition and date a figure refers to.

questions.stem: The Bandra-Kurla Complex in Mumbai is a planned business district developed away from the old southern CBD. This shows that Mumbai is becoming:
options: more monocentric, with all offices moving back to the southern tip
less urbanised, with businesses relocating to rural villages
less connected, with global firms leaving the city altogether
more polycentric, with new centres nearer the northern suburbs
questions.explanation: New centres such as the Bandra-Kurla Complex bring offices closer to where most people live in the north and ease pressure on the historic CBD.

questions.stem: Much of Mumbai's population growth over the 20th century came from:
options: rural-urban migration from Maharashtra and poorer states such as Bihar
international migration from Europe after India's independence in 1947
a sharp rise in the birth rate, with migration playing no part at all
the return of residents from Navi Mumbai to the southern peninsula
questions.explanation: Migrants seeking work in the port, textile mills and later services came from rural Maharashtra and other states. Natural increase also contributed, but migration has been a major driver.

questions.stem: Mumbai is often called India's financial capital because it:
options: hosts the Reserve Bank of India and the main stock exchanges
is the seat of India's national parliament and central government
produces most of India's rice and wheat in its surrounding farmland
is the largest city in the world by both area and population
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India, the Bombay Stock Exchange and the National Stock Exchange are in Mumbai, along with many corporate headquarters. The national parliament is in New Delhi.

questions.stem: Which political role does Mumbai hold within India?
options: capital of the state of Gujarat
a union territory run from Delhi
capital of Maharashtra state
capital of the Republic of India
questions.explanation: Mumbai is Maharashtra's state capital. India's national capital is New Delhi, and Gujarat's capital is Gandhinagar.

questions.stem: From the 1980s, many of central Mumbai's cotton textile mills closed, and much of the mill land was later redeveloped into offices, shopping malls and luxury apartments. This change best illustrates:
options: industrialisation driven by new factories opening in the inner city
counterurbanisation as mill workers moved to new rural factories
suburbanisation of heavy industry into the central business district
deindustrialisation, then gentrification and a shift to services
questions.explanation: The decline of manufacturing (deindustrialisation) left valuable central land, which was redeveloped for higher-income uses, displacing former mill communities. The economy shifted towards finance and services.

questions.stem: Mumbai's film industry, commonly known as Bollywood, and its call centres and IT firms serving overseas clients, are examples of Mumbai's:
options: regional and global linkages through cultural and economic ties
isolation from global markets due to strict trade barriers
dependence on agriculture as its main source of employment
role as a primate city that controls India's entire economy
questions.explanation: Films, services and finance link Mumbai to audiences and businesses across India and the world. India is not dominated by a single primate city; Delhi, Kolkata and others are also very large.

questions.stem: Mumbai's port, now centred on Jawaharlal Nehru Port at Nhava Sheva across the harbour, handles a large share of India's container trade. Geographically this shows Mumbai's role as:
options: a gateway linking India's economy to global trade
a city with no economic links beyond its region
a centre of subsistence farming and fishing only
a political capital with no commercial functions
questions.explanation: The port connects Indian producers and consumers with world markets, a gateway function that helped Mumbai grow. The move across the harbour reflects the lack of space and deep water on the peninsula.

questions.stem: India's 2011 census recorded roughly two-fifths of Greater Mumbai's population living in slums. Which challenge is most closely linked to this?
options: a shortage of workers, because few migrants have moved to the city
a lack of affordable formal housing as land prices soar
a surplus of empty housing, with more homes than people needing them
very low population density across the whole of the island city
questions.explanation: Scarce land and high prices put formal housing beyond most low-income households, so many live in informal settlements with poor sanitation and insecure tenure.

questions.stem: Dharavi, one of Asia's largest informal settlements, lies near the Bandra-Kurla Complex. Which statement best describes it?
options: a planned industrial estate run by a single transnational corporation
a dense area with a busy informal economy of recycling, leather and pottery
an empty area of wetlands protected from all development and economic activity
a wealthy gated suburb of detached houses on large, landscaped blocks
questions.explanation: Dharavi is home to many small-scale industries and workshops that produce goods sold across India and abroad, alongside severe overcrowding and poor sanitation. Its central location makes the land very valuable.

questions.stem: On 26 July 2005, more than 900 mm of rain fell in 24 hours at Mumbai's Santacruz weather station, and large areas flooded. Which human factors worsened the flooding?
options: the absence of any rainfall records, so the monsoon arrived unexpectedly
the construction of too many parks and wetlands across the city
the city's location on a high plateau far from the sea or any river
old, low-capacity drains blocked by waste, and the loss of mangroves
questions.explanation: Mumbai's colonial-era storm drains were designed for far less intense rain, many were choked with rubbish, and building on mangroves and along the Mithi River removed natural flood storage.

questions.stem: Mumbai's suburban trains carry millions of passengers a day and are often packed far beyond their design capacity. This is mainly a result of:
options: very low car ownership in a city with no road network at all
the absence of any commuters, because most residents work from home
a policy of running only one train per hour to reduce noise in suburbs
a long, narrow city where homes and jobs are linked by a few rail lines
questions.explanation: The peninsula's shape funnels huge numbers of commuters onto a small number of north-south lines, causing severe crowding and accidents. Road traffic is also heavily congested.

questions.stem: In large cities such as Mumbai, luxury apartment towers often stand next to informal settlements. This is a clear example of:
options: spatial inequality in housing, services and quality of life
spatial equality, with all residents receiving the same services
rural decline, with services withdrawn from the urban area
urban sprawl at the edge of a low-density metropolitan area
questions.explanation: Spatial inequality is the uneven distribution of wealth, housing and services across a city. In Mumbai, extreme wealth and poverty exist side by side.

questions.stem: Mumbai's Deonar dumping ground, one of India's oldest landfills, has suffered large fires that spread smoke over nearby informal settlements. Which statement best links this challenge to spatial inequality?
options: poorer communities bear more of the health costs of the city's waste
all residents of the city are equally exposed to smoke from the landfill
the landfill was located in the wealthiest suburb to share the burden
waste disposal has no effect on the health of people living nearby
questions.explanation: Waste facilities are often sited near low-income neighbourhoods, which then suffer the worst air pollution and health effects. This environmental injustice is one form of spatial inequality.

questions.stem: Under Mumbai's Slum Rehabilitation Authority scheme, a developer rehouses slum residents in free apartments on part of a site and gains extra floor space to sell at market prices. A key criticism of this approach is that:
options: the scheme moves all slum residents to rural villages outside the city
high-rise rehousing can disrupt livelihoods and create poorly kept towers
developers receive no benefit, so no slum sites have ever been redeveloped
residents are required to buy their new apartments at full market price
questions.explanation: The scheme uses private profit to fund rehousing, but critics note cramped, poorly lit towers, lost space for home-based work, exclusion of residents without paperwork and developers capturing much of the land value.

questions.stem: Mumbai has been building a network of metro lines alongside its suburban railway. The main aim of this response is to:
options: reduce crowding and travel times while cutting car use and pollution
replace all buses and trains with private cars over the next decade
move the city's whole population out to Navi Mumbai and Thane
reduce the number of jobs in the city so fewer people need to travel
questions.explanation: Metro lines add capacity on east-west and north-south routes, easing pressure on the overcrowded suburban network and roads. This improves quality of life and supports more sustainable transport.

questions.stem: After the 2005 floods, Mumbai began widening and upgrading its storm water drains and gave greater protection to mangroves. Which statement best evaluates this response?
options: it increases flood risk, because mangroves block rivers from reaching the sea
it is irrelevant to flooding, which depends only on the amount of rainfall
it reduces flood risk, but heavier rain and growth need ongoing work
it removes all flood risk permanently, so no further action will be needed
questions.explanation: Larger drains and mangrove buffers improve drainage and storm protection, but heavier monsoon downpours, sea level rise and continued construction mean flooding still occurs. Evaluations weigh partial success against remaining risk.

questions.stem: Community groups in Mumbai, working with NGOs, have designed and managed shared toilet blocks in informal settlements. This response is significant because it:
options: is run by a transnational corporation for profit in each settlement
involves residents directly, improving sanitation at low cost
replaces the need for any government spending on water or sewerage
moves residents to new housing estates on the edge of the city
questions.explanation: Community-led sanitation gives residents control over design and maintenance, so facilities suit local needs and are better kept. It works alongside, not instead of, municipal infrastructure.

questions.stem: A planner must choose between clearing an informal settlement and rehousing residents far away, or upgrading the settlement in place with water, drains and secure tenure. Why is in-situ upgrading often judged more sustainable?
options: it removes all residents from hazardous land at no cost to anyone
it keeps residents near jobs and social networks while improving services
it is always more expensive, so it attracts more international aid funding
it allows the land to be sold quickly to developers for luxury apartments
questions.explanation: Relocation to distant estates often cuts people off from work, schools and support networks, and many return to the city. Upgrading in place improves living conditions while keeping livelihoods intact.

questions.stem: The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, a sea bridge of about 22 km opened in 2024, connects the island city with the mainland near Navi Mumbai. Which opportunity does it offer?
options: faster links to new jobs, housing and port areas on the mainland
a ban on all road traffic travelling into central Mumbai each day
a new airport built entirely on the bridge deck above the harbour
the removal of the need for any other public transport in the city
questions.explanation: By cutting travel times across the harbour, the bridge supports growth on the mainland and links to the port, helping spread development beyond the crowded peninsula. Critics raise concerns about its effects on the harbour's mudflats and birdlife.

questions.stem: Which indicator would best show whether responses in a large city are reducing spatial inequality?
options: the number of new skyscrapers completed in the central business district
the total population of the metropolitan region recorded at one census
the volume of international flights arriving at the city's airport each year
changes over time in access to water and housing across districts
questions.explanation: Spatial inequality is about differences between areas, so the best indicator compares access to services and housing across districts over time. Skyscrapers and flights measure growth, not distribution.

questions.stem: Which process describes wealthier households moving into a run-down inner-city area, renovating housing and raising property values?
options: informalisation
gentrification
suburbanisation
counterurbanisation
questions.explanation: Gentrification brings investment to inner areas but can displace lower-income residents and businesses, as on former mill land in central Mumbai.

questions.stem: Mumbai, like many large cities in developing countries, grew rapidly with many residents in informal housing, whereas Tokyo grew earlier with more planned infrastructure. Which statement best explains this difference?
options: informal housing is required by Indian law for all new city residents
in Mumbai, growth outpaced the provision of housing and services
Tokyo has never experienced rural-urban migration in its entire history
Mumbai has a far smaller population than Tokyo, so it needs less housing
questions.explanation: Where population grows faster than governments can provide formal housing, water and transport, informal settlements fill the gap. Tokyo also grew through migration, but rising incomes allowed formal infrastructure to keep pace.

questions.stem: Rising temperatures and heavier monsoon rain are expected to increase challenges for Mumbai. Which response best combines sustainability with quality of life?
options: relocating all industry to the coast, where land is cheapest and least protected
protecting mangroves, adding green space and upgrading drains in poor areas
replacing remaining wetlands with housing to meet demand as quickly as possible
building sea walls only around the wealthiest suburbs to protect investment
questions.explanation: Nature-based protection and green space reduce flood and heat risk, and prioritising poorer areas addresses spatial inequality. Building on wetlands increases risk, and protecting only wealthy areas widens inequality.

questions.stem: A large city that is a major node in global networks of finance, trade and communication is called:
options: a world city
a regional centre
a satellite town
a remote settlement
questions.explanation: World or global cities, such as Mumbai, London and Tokyo, have command and control functions in the global economy. Regional centres serve a surrounding rural area.

questions.stem: A student compares maps of Mumbai's built-up area from 1990 and 2020 drawn from satellite images. The comparison is most useful for showing:
options: the cultural traditions of the city's residents
the daily income earned by informal workers
the rate and direction of the city's growth
the number of people living in each apartment
questions.explanation: Comparing images from two dates shows how far and in which directions urban land has expanded, such as northwards and onto the mainland. Household size, culture and income need census or survey data.

questions.stem: Mumbai's planners promote new housing and jobs in Navi Mumbai and the wider region rather than on the crowded peninsula. This strategy mainly aims to:
options: close the port and convert all industrial land into farmland
spread growth across the region to ease congestion in the core
stop all population growth in the metropolitan region within a few years
move India's national government and parliament from Delhi to Mumbai
questions.explanation: Decentralising growth to planned centres reduces pressure on transport, housing and services in the core. Success depends on good transport links so that new centres attract jobs, not just housing.

questions.stem: When evaluating a large city's responses, why should a geographer consider the perspectives of different groups, such as informal workers, developers and the municipal government?
options: perspectives are opinions, so they should never be used as evidence in geography
responses create winners and losers, so effectiveness depends on who is asked
every group always agrees on the best response, so perspectives are identical
only the government's view matters because it pays for all urban projects
questions.explanation: A redevelopment may suit developers and the city's finances while displacing informal workers. Comparing perspectives shows the social, economic and environmental trade-offs of each response.
